question_text:
A 68-year-old man presents to the clinic for a regular health checkup. He is hypertensive and was diagnosed with congestive heart failure last year. He has hyperlipidemia but does not take any medication for it.
Although he takes his antihypertensive medications regularly, his blood pressure recordings at home tend to range between 150/98 and 160/90 mm Hg. Today, his blood pressure is 147/96 mm Hg.
The doctor decides to add indapamide to his medication list and asks the patient to follow up within 2 weeks. The patient is compliant with the medication. He comes back to the physician in Just one week complaining of muscle cramping and weakness.
Which of the following is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
explanation:
Indapamide is a thiazide-like diuretic, which acts act on the proximal part of the distal convoluted tubule and inhibits the sodium/chloride cotransport system.

Thiazide-like diuretics have the same physiologic function as thiazide diuretics, but they have a different mechanism.

The complications that can arise are hyperglycemia, hyperuricemia, hypercalcemia, hyperlipidemia, and hypokalemia.

Hyperglycemia is caused by the inhibition of insulin secretion due to hypokalemia produced by thiazide.

Inhibition of the sodium/chloride cotransport system results in lower intracellular sodium in tubular cells. This leads to an increase in activity of the sodium/calcium exchanger which promotes increased calcium resorption.

The hyperlipldemla may be secondary to decreased insulin secretion. Hyperuricemia occurs because thiazide diuretics use organic acid transporters in the proximal tubule that are also used by uric acid.

This leads to underexcretion of uric acid, resulting in hyperuricemia. Muscle weakness and cramping in this patient is most likely due to hypokalemia.

Option A: Thiazide diuretics reduce the excretion of calcium from the body and can result in hypercalcemia.

Option B: Hyperglycemia is a complication that is commonly seen with thiazide diuretics.

Option C: Hyperlipidemia is another complication seen with thiazide diuretics, but it is unlikely to be the cause for the symptoms seen with this patient.

Learning objective:

The three main thiazide-like diuretics are metolazone, chlorthalidone, and indapamide. They inhibit the Na'/C1- cotransport system and decrease the active reabsorption of Na' and CI-.

The actions of thiazide-like diuretics include:

  • Increased excretion of K' & H'
  • Decreased excretion of uric acid
  • Increased excretion of Mg"
  • Decreased excretion of Ca-
  • Moderate vasodilator effect

Thus, complications that can occur with thiazide diuretics include hyperglycemia, hyperuricemia, hypercalcemia, hyperlipidemia, and hypokalemia.

Reference: Guyton & Hall, 14th edition pg no. 571

question_text:
A 65-year-old male patient presents to the emergency department with chest pain and shortness of breath. His medical history includes hypertension and diabetes. Upon examination, he shows signs of peripheral edema. An ECG reveals left ventricular hypertrophy.
Which of the following mechanisms is most likely contributing to the patient's symptoms related to vascular physiology?
explanation:
• Left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) is typically caused by increased afterload, the resistance the heart must overcome during systole. Chronic hypertension increases afterload, leading to LVH as the heart works harder to pump blood.
  • The peripheral edema suggests fluid overload, often seen in heart failure due to the heart's inability to effectively pump against the increased afterload.

Why Not Other Options

  • A (Increased venous return): This leads to increased preload, not afterload, and doesn't explain the LVH and peripheral edema.
  • B (Decreased systemic vascular resistance): This would result in lower blood pressure, which contradicts the patient's hypertensive state.
  • C (Increased preload): Although preload might be increased in heart failure, the primary issue here is afterload, leading to LVH.

Key Takeaways

  • Main Mechanism: Increased afterload due to hypertension is driving the LVH and associated heart failure symptoms.

question_text: Below are two vessels shown. Assuming the pressure along both the vessels is the same and both of them follow linear flow pattern. What will the amount of blood flow in A compared to B
explanation:
Blood flow (F) inside vessel depends on:

  • Pressure difference (PA - PB) - directly related
  • Viscosity of the fluid (η) - inversely related
    • Viscosity is a measure of a fluid's resistance to flow
    • A fluid with low viscosity flows easily. Such fluids are called Newtonian fluid. Example is water
    • A fluid with high viscosity flows resists motion. Such fluids are called Non-newtonian fluid. Example is blood
    • Fahraeus-Lindqvist effect: This effect is seen mainly in capillaries where RBCs flow in the center which leaves cell free plasma near the vessel wall. So, the viscosity change per unit change in hematocrit is much less in capillaries
  • Radius of the vessel (r4) - directly related
  • Length of the vessel (L) - inversely related
  • Interrelation of these factors are expressed in Poiseuille- Hagen formula which is:

F = (PA-PB) * πr4/8η L

  • Since, length is doubled and diameter is doubled in vessel A, its flow will be:

F = 24/2=16/2 = 8 times

question_text: A 50yr old man presents with paresthesia, Hb- 6.8 g/dl. Peripheral smear shows macrocytes and neutrophils with hyper segmented nuclei. Endoscopy reveals atrophic gastritis. Which of the deficiency is most likely?
explanation:
Pernicious Anemia a Type 2 Hypersensitivity in which Abs are formed against Intrinsic Factor thus Inhibits the Binding of intrinsic factor+B12

  • Pernicious anemia commonly accompanies gastric atrophy and achlorhydria. Normal gastric secretions contain a glycoprotein called intrinsic factor, secreted by the same parietal cells that secrete hydrochloric acid.
  • Intrinsic factor must be present for adequate absorption of vitamin B 12 from the ileum. That is, intrinsic factor combines with vitamin B12 in the stomach and protects it from being digested and destroyed as it passes into the small intestine.
  • Then, when the intrinsic factor-vitamin B 12 complex reaches the terminal ileum, the intrinsic factor binds with receptors on the ileal epithelial surface, which in turn makes it possible for the vitamin B 12 to be absorbed.
  • In the absence of intrinsic factor, only about 1/50th of the vitamin B 12 is absorbed. In addition, without intrinsic factor, an adequate amount of vitamin B 12 is not made available from the foods to cause young, newly forming red blood cells to mature in the bone marrow. The result is pernicious anemia

question_text: A 45-year-old woman presents to the clinic with episodes of palpitations, severe headache, and sweating that occur intermittently, particularly when she is under stress. She reports feeling anxious during these episodes. Physical examination reveals elevated blood pressure (160/100 mmHg) and tachycardia. A 24-hour urinary collection shows elevated levels of catecholamines and their metabolites. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• Pheochromocytoma:
    • Characteristics: Tumor of the adrenal medulla secreting catecholamines (epinephrine and norepinephrine).
    • Symptoms:
      • Episodic palpitations, severe headache, sweating, and anxiety during episodes, particularly under stress.
      • Hypertension and tachycardia upon examination.
      • Laboratory Findings: Elevated catecholamines and metabolites in 24-hour urine collection confirm the diagnosis.
    • The combination of episodic symptoms and elevated catecholamines is classic for pheochromocytoma.

Why not other options:

  • Primary Hyperaldosteronism (Conn's Syndrome):
    • Incorrect. This condition involves excessive aldosterone leading to hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis, but does not cause episodic symptoms like palpitations, sweating, or anxiety, nor does it significantly increase catecholamines.
  • Cushing's Syndrome:
    • Incorrect. Characterized by elevated cortisol leading to persistent symptoms like weight gain, hypertension, and fat redistribution. Symptoms are typically not episodic, and the patient's presentation does not match.
  • Secondary Hypertension:
    • Incorrect. Refers to hypertension caused by identifiable conditions. While the patient has hypertension, the episodic nature of symptoms and significant catecholamine levels suggest a specific disorder rather than a generic cause of secondary hypertension, which would not typically involve anxiety or sweating episodes.

Key Takeaways:

  • The patient's episodic symptoms(palpitations, headaches, sweating) alongside elevated catecholamines confirm a diagnosis of pheochromocytoma.
  • Understanding the relationship between symptom patterns and hormone levels is crucial for accurate diagnosis in adrenal gland disorders.

question_text: A 42-year-old male complains of burning sensation in the epigastric region, which is relieved after a meal. The patient was diagnosed with peptic ulcer. Which of the following will increase gastric secretion

Option D: Ach acts on M3 receptors on the basolateral membrane of stomach and increases intra cellular calcium which in turn activates protein kinase which in turn increases the activity of H+/K+ ATPase and increases gastric secretion

Phases of Gastric Acid Secretion:

question_text: What does the 2nd phase of saliva secretion involve?
option_a: Active Na absorption, Passive Cl absorption, Active K secretion, active & passive secretion of HCO3
option_b: Passive Na absorption, Passive Cl absorption, Active K secretion, active & passive secretion of HCO3
option_c: Active Na absorption, Active Cl absorption, Active K secretion, active & passive secretion of HCO3
option_d: Active Na absorption, Passive Cl absorption, Passive K secretion, active & passive secretion of HCO3
explanation:
Salivary secretion is a two-stage operation:

The first stage involves the acini.

The second stage involves the salivary ducts.

First, Na+ is actively reabsorbed from all the salivary ducts and K+ is actively secreted in exchange for Na+. However, there is excess Na+ reabsorption compared with K+ secretion, which creates electrical negativity of about -70 millivolts in the salivary ducts. So this negativity causes Cl- to be reabsorbed passively.

Second, HCO3- is secreted by the ductal epithelium into the lumen of the duct. This secretion is partly caused by passive exchange of bicarbonate for Cl- but it may also result partly from an active secretory process.

question_text: A 23-year-old female patient comes to the OPD and complains of sialorrhea. Which of the following statements is not true about salivary secretion

Salivary secretion has a pH of 7.0 and neutralises acidity from stomach when gastric juice is regurgitated into esophagus in heartburn and relieves it.

The amylase in saliva partially digests starch.

IgA and lysozymes in saliva protect the oral cavity against bacteria.

Salivary secretion is regulated by parasympathetic input, triggered by stimuli like chewing or the sight of food, has a neutral pH of 7.0 to neutralize gastric acid during heartburn, contains amylase for starch digestion, and protects the oral cavity with IgA and lysozymes.

question_text: Which of the following factors was shown to inhibit insulin secretion in studies on insulin regulation?
explanation:
Explanation

Epinephrine can exert both stimulatory and inhibitory effects on insulin release depending on the body's metabolic needs.

  • Under stress, exercise, or hypoglycemia, epinephrine acts mainly through α-adrenergic receptor activation, which suppresses insulin secretion. This ensures higher blood glucose availability to meet immediate energy demands.
  • In contrast, during rest and digestion when epinephrine levels are low, insulin secretion is allowed to proceed, facilitating glucose uptake and storage.

Explanation of other options:

Gastric Inhibitory Polypeptide (Option B):

  • A gastrointestinal hormone (also called GIP)
  • Acts as an incretin, stimulating insulin release after oral glucose intake
  • Hence, it promotes rather than inhibits insulin secretion

Acetylcholine (Option C):

  • Released via parasympathetic stimulation
  • Enhances insulin secretion by increasing intracellular calcium in pancreatic β-cells
  • Therefore, it is a stimulator, not inhibitor of insulin release

None of the above (Option D):Incorrect because epinephrine is indeed a recognized inhibitor of insulin secretion

question_text: A 45-year-old patient undergoes complete ileal and partial jejunal resection due to Crohn's disease. Which of the following deficiencies is he most likely to develop in the long term?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Vitamin B12 (cobalamin)is absorbed primarily in the terminal ileum after binding to intrinsic factor (IF) secreted by gastric parietal cells.
  • Complete ileal resection→ impaired B12 absorption → megaloblastic anemia and neurological symptoms (paresthesia, memory impairment).
  • Jejunal resectionaffects absorption of carbohydrates, proteins, fats, and some vitamins, but does not significantly impact B12 absorption, which occurs mainly in the ileum.
  • Therefore, Vitamin B12 deficiencyis the most immediate and predictable outcome.
  • Ileum resection:B12, bile salts → fat malabsorption, steatorrhea
  • Jejunum resection:Carbs, proteins, water-soluble vitamins → malnutrition, diarrhea

Explanation of Other Options:

Folic acid deficiency (Option A):

Absorbed in proximal small intestine (duodenum, jejunum).

Only a minor portion of the jejunum is resected → folate absorption may be partially affected, but B12 deficiency is more likely.

Gastric ulcer (Option C):

Not directly caused by ileal or jejunal resection.

Gastric acid secretion or IF may be affected indirectly by B12 deficiency but does not cause ulceration.

Constipation (Option D):

May occur due to decreased bowel length or malabsorption, but not the most likely or direct consequence compared to B12 deficiency.

Key Takeaway Points:

  1. Site of Vitamin Absorption in Small Intestine
  2. Clinical Correlation:
    • Vitamin B12 deficiency signs:
      • Megaloblastic anemia (macrocytosis)
      • Neurological: peripheral neuropathy, subacute combined degeneration of spinal cord
    • Management:Lifelong B12 supplementation (oral if some ileum remains; otherwise parenteral).

question_text: A patient with history of celiac disease comes to your clinic presenting a pattern of deficiencies indicating malabsorption syndrome. What would be the possible change in diet plan that you would suggest with the symptomatic treatments?
option_d: Food rich in trans fatty acids
explanation:
Option A: Celiac disease occurs in genetically predisposed individuals in whom gluten and closely related proteins cause intestinal T cells to mount an inappropriate immune response that damages the intestinal epithelial cells and results in a loss of villi and a flattening of the mucosa associated with crypt hyperplasia. In celiac disease, the mucosa returns to normal if foods containing gluten are strictly excluded from the diet, although this may be difficult to achieve.

Foods containing gluten: Barley, rice, oats, wheat (BROW).

Antigliadin/antiendomyseal/antiTTG antibodies are produced in celiac disease.

HLA association: HLADQ2

Option B: (Food rich in proteins): While beneficial, it doesn't address the underlying gluten issue in celiac disease.

Option C: (Carbohydrate-rich foods): Many carbohydrates can contain gluten, which would exacerbate symptoms.

Option D: (Food rich in trans fatty acids): Trans fats are generally unhealthy and do not help with malabsorption or celiac disease management.

Key takeaways:

Patients with celiac disease must avoid gluten to manage malabsorption and prevent symptoms.

He was diagnosed with end-stage renal disease 6 months ago and is currently on dialysis. His wife, who is accompanying him today, adds that he is not compliant with his medicines. On examination, the patient has a waddling gait. Hypotonia of all the limbs is evident on neurologic examination. Diffuse bone tenderness is remarkable. X-ray of his legs reveal osteopenia and osseous resorption. The final step of activation of the deficient vitamin in this patient occurs by which of the following enzymes?
explanation:
Diabetes mellitus is the most common cause of chronic kidney disease (CKD) followed by hypertension. This patient is most likely suffering from osteomalacia which occurs due to vitamin D deficiency after epiphyseal closure (in adulthood).

Vitamin D deficiency is one of the most common complications of end-stage renal disease as the kidneys play an important role in vitamin D activation (see image below).

Lab results in patients with osteomalacia usually show low calcium, low phosphate, and high alkaline phosphatase (ALP).

Cholecalciferol (vitamin D3) can be obtained from food (e.g., liver, fish oil) or endogenously (under the effect of sunlight).

For vitamin D to be in the most active form, it goes through two steps of hydroxylation, The first step of hydroxylation occurs in the liver CYP-450 system, in which vitamin D is converted to 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25-[OH]D; calcidiol)

The second step of hydroxylation occurs in the proximal tubules of the kidneys by 1-a-hydroxylase (synthesized under the effect of parathyroid hormone), and the active form of vitamin D is formed (1,25-(OH) 2-D; calcitriol) Vitamin D is inactivated by 24, 25 hydroxylase into inactive metabolite (choice E)

Functions of vitamin D:

Increase calcium and phosphorus reabsorption from small intestines and kidneys Mineralization of epiphyseal cartilage and osteoid Stimulate the maturation of cells, including immune system cells Calcium and phosphate disorders are common in patients with end-stage renal disease and can be treated as follows:

If calcium is low:

Calcium supplements can treat hypocalcemia when given between meals and binds phosphate when given with meais Calcitriol (1, 25-dihydroxyvitamin D) or vitamin D analogs (being introduced in the future) If calcium and phosphate are high: Phosphate binder (sevelamer) should be given

Option A: 7-a-hydroxylase conducts the first and rate-limiting step in bile acid synthesis, which is the conversion of cholesterol to 7-alpha-hydroxycholesterol.

Fibrates inhibit this enzyme, leading to more cholesterol in the bile and increased risk of cholesterol gallstones.

Option C: a-1-antitrypsin is a protease inhibitor (also known as -1- antiproteinase). Deficiency of this enzyme can cause liver cirrhosis and panacinar emphysema (targets the lower lobe of the lung).

Option D: a-Glucosidase is an enzyme located on the brush border of the small intestine, and it plays a role in carbohydrate digestion and absorption.

Glucosidase inhibitors (e.g., Acarbose, Miglitol) are a group of oral antidiabetic drugs used for type il diabetes mellitus. Side effects of this group of drugs include diarrhea and flatulence.

Learning objective: Vitamin D deficiency is common in patients with end-stage renal disease. Vitamin D deficiency in adults (after epiphyseal closure) causes osteomalacia and rickets in children before epiphyseal closure.

Manifestations of osteomalacia are less dramatic than rickets and include diffuse bone pain, muscular weakness, hypotonia, and increased risk of bone fractures.

question_text: An infant is diagnosed with congenital absence of enterokinase. What would be likely complication due to this congenital defect?

question_text: A person goes to Mount Abu for three days which he had several bouts of vomiting. He was diagnosed with motion sickness, which was the cause of his vomiting. Which of the following is not correct about the changes that occur during Vomiting?
option_d: The breath is held in mid inspiration
explanation:
Option A: Vomiting is an example of central regulation of gut motility functions. Vomiting starts with salivation and the sensation of nausea. Reverse peristalsis empties material from the upper part of the small intestine into the stomach. The glottis closes, preventing aspiration of vomitus into the trachea. The breath is held in mid inspiration. The muscles of the abdominal wall contract, and because the chest is held in a fixed position, the contraction increases intra-abdominal pressure. The lower esophageal sphincter and the esophagus relax, and the gastric contents are ejected.

Option B: (The lower esophageal sphincter relaxes): This is correct; the lower esophageal sphincter relaxes to allow the contents to move from the stomach into the esophagus.

Option C: (Abdominal muscles contract): This is also correct; contraction of the abdominal muscles helps to forcefully expel the stomach contents during vomiting.

Option D: (The breath is held in mid-inspiration): This is correct; holding the breath during vomiting helps to prevent aspiration.

Key takeaways:

Vomiting is a regulated process involving salivation, nausea, reverse peristalsis, glottis closure to prevent aspiration, abdominal contraction to increase pressure, and relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter to expel gastric contents.

question_text: During the placement of an NG tube, the Lower esophageal sphincter of a patient was found to be deficient in myenteric plexus. The release of NO and VIP is defective. What kind of abnormalities would the patient face?

explanation:
Option B: The absence of myenteric plexus and  NO and VIP causes the resting tone of lower esophageal sphincter (LES) to be increased. These results in non-relaxation of the LES called achalasia. The tight sphincter will cause difficulty in passage of food from esophagus to stomach. It causes indigestion and infection in the lower esophagus

GERD is the opposite condition where incompetent LES allows acid reflux into the esophagus. It can cause heart burn and infection in the lower esophagus with ulceration.

Since the food cannot pass down from esophagus in achalasia, it is expelled out by vomiting reflex.

Diarrhea is caused by increased intestinal motility.

Other options:

Option A: GERD: While a deficient LES can contribute to GERD, the primary issue here is difficulty in food passage due to impaired motility, not reflux.

Option C: Decreased vomiting reflex: The myenteric plexus primarily affects gut motility; it does not directly cause decreased vomiting reflex.

Option D: Frequent diarrhea: This is unrelated to the condition described, as it primarily involves esophageal motility rather than intestinal function.

Key takeaways:

Absence of the myenteric plexus and reduced NO and VIP leads to increased lower esophageal sphincter tone, causing achalasia and difficulty in food passage, unlike GERD, where the sphincter is incompetent.

Identify the movement taking place in the intestine?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Peristaltic movement refers to coordinated, wave-like contractions of the intestinal smooth muscle.
  • These contractions move luminal contents (chyme) forward along the gastrointestinal tract.
  • It is the primary propulsive movement of the intestine, essential for normal digestion and absorption.
  • Triggered by the myenteric plexus (Auerbach's plexus) in response to local distension of the intestinal wall.

Explanation of Other options:

Segmented movement (Option A):

  • Non-propulsive contraction.
  • Helps in mixing chyme with digestive enzymes and exposes it to the intestinal mucosa for absorption.
  • Does not move contents forward significantly.

Passive diffusion (Option C):

  • A transport mechanism across membranes, not a motor activity of the intestine.
  • Refers to movement of small molecules (e.g., gases, lipids) across the epithelium down a concentration gradient.

Intersegmental contraction (Option D):

  • Not a standard physiological term for intestinal motility.
  • Sometimes used to describe localized contractions between segments, but not a recognized primary motor activity.

Key Takeaway Points:

  • Intestinal movements are of two main types: propulsive (peristalsis) and mixing (segmentation).
  • Peristalsis is essential for moving food along the GI tract.
  • Coordinated by the enteric nervous system, particularly the myenteric plexus.

question_text: What is the name of the movement that occurs in the intestine?
explanation:
Explanation:

Peristalsis is a wave-like muscular contraction occurring within the smooth muscle layers of the gastrointestinal (GI) tract, including the intestines. This movement propels food and chyme in a forward (unidirectional) motion, helping move contents through the digestive system.

Trigger Mechanism: Peristalsis begins as a reflex response to the stretching of the intestinal wall caused by the presence of contents in the lumen.

Location: It occurs throughout the entire GI tract, from the esophagus to the rectum.

Movement Pattern:

  • Stretching initiates circular muscle contraction just behind the bolus and relaxation ahead of it.
  • The resulting peristaltic wave moves from the oral (mouth) end to the caudal (anal) end,
  • Propelling intestinal contents at speeds ranging from 2 to 25 cm/s.

Regulation:

  • Although autonomic nerves influence it, peristalsis is primarily controlled by the enteric nervous system and can function independently of external innervation.
  • Local stretch triggers the release of serotonin, which activates sensory neurons and stimulates the myenteric plexus.
  • Cholinergic neurons within the plexus coordinate muscle responses:
    • In the retrograde direction (behind the bolus): release substance P and acetylcholine, causing muscle contraction.
    • In the anterograde direction (ahead of the bolus): stimulate neurons that release nitric oxide (NO) and vasoactive intestinal polypeptide (VIP), leading to muscle relaxation.

Functional Integration: Peristalsis represents a classic example of the coordinated control by the enteric nervous system, ensuring the effective movement of contents through the GI tract.

Neurotransmitters Involved in Peristalsis

Explanation of Other Options:

Segmented Movement (Option A): Segmental contractions are rhythmic, localized contractions that primarily mix the intestinal contents rather than propel them. They occur mainly in the small intestine for enhanced nutrient absorption but do not move contents forward significantly.

Intersegmental Contraction (Option C): This term does not specifically describe a recognized physiological pattern of intestinal motility. It may suggest contractions between intestinal segments, but true motility patterns are categorized as peristalsis, segmentation, or mass movement.

Diffusion (Option D): Diffusion is a passive process of molecular movement down a concentration gradient, not an active muscular movement of the intestine. It pertains to nutrient transport across membranes, not intestinal motility.

Reference:

https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12966154/

question_text: In a period between meals, the intestine is relatively quiescent, but every 90 minutes it is swept through by a large peristaltic wave. Which hormone is responsible for such peristaltic wave?
explanation:
Option D: In the period between meals, the intestine is relatively quiescent but every 90 minutes it is swept through by a large peristaltic wave triggered by hormone motilin. The migratory motor complex (MMC) presumably serves a housekeeping function. MMC also known as hunger/housekeeping contractions. MMC progress at a rate of 5cm/min.

Option A: (Somatostatin): This hormone inhibits gastric acid secretion and other gastrointestinal functions but does not stimulate peristalsis.

Option B: (Secretin): Primarily regulates water homeostasis and bicarbonate secretion in the pancreas but does not trigger peristaltic waves.

Option C: (Nitrous oxide): it is not the primary hormone responsible for the migrating motor complex.

Key takeaways:

Motilin is responsible for triggering the large peristaltic waves (migrating motor complex) that occur in the intestine approximately every 90-120 minutes during the fasting state.

question_text:
Select the correct statements regarding the enteric nervous system from the options given below.
1. Vagus is the only afferent from gut
2. Functions independent of brain and SC
3. Myenteric plexus in the lamina propria
4. Exclusively under the influence of nerves
5. Parasympathetic connects enteric to CNS
explanation:
Explanation:

The enteric nervous system (ENS) is an autonomous network capable of functioning independently of the brain and spinal cord, regulating intestinal motility, secretion, and blood flow.

In addition to the vagus nerve, spinal afferents also transmit pain and reflex signals from the gut.

The myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus lies between the circular and longitudinal muscle layers, rather than within the lamina propria.

The ENS is modulated by hormones and local chemical factors, not solely by neural input. The parasympathetic system links the ENS with the central nervous system, helping to regulate its functions.

Components of the Enteric Nervous System:

Explanation of other options:

1,2,3 (Option A): The vagus is not the sole afferent pathway, and the myenteric plexus is not located in the lamina propria.

1,4 (Option B): The ENS isn't controlled only by neural input; hormones and local factors also play a role.

1,3 (Option C): Both the claim that only the vagus provides afferents and the statement about the myenteric plexus location are false.

Key Takeaways:

  • ENS can function independently of the CNS.
  • Myenteric plexus lies between muscle layers, not in lamina propria.
  • Gut control is modulated by both neural and hormonal inputs.

question_text: A 35-year-old patient underwent endoscopic evaluation of the gastrointestinal tract for recurrent abdominal discomfort and altered bowel habits. The arrow-marked structure in the provided histology slide needs to be identified.
explanation:
Explanation:

The histology image corresponds to the duodenum.

Key identification features:

  • The intestinal wall consists of four layers.
  • The mucosa shows broad villi lined by simple columnar epithelium with microvilli and goblet cells.
  • Crypts of Lieberkuhn are present in the mucosa.
  • Most importantly, the submucosa contains Brunner's glands, which secrete alkaline mucus to neutralize gastric acid.
  • The arrow-marked structure is therefore Brunner's gland.

Explanation of other options:

Crypts of Lieberkuhn (Option C): These are tubular glands located in the mucosa between villi throughout the small intestine. While they are present in the duodenum, the arrow is not pointing to them, ruling out this option.

Interstitial cells of Cajal (Option B): Specialized pacemaker cells within the intestinal smooth muscle responsible for generating basal electrical rhythm (BER). They do not appear as submucosal glandular structures, hence incorrect here.

Peyer's patches (Option D): Aggregated lymphoid nodules predominantly seen in the terminal ileum, not in the duodenum. Since the image is from the duodenum, this option is ruled out.

question_text: Where are the primary pacemaker cells responsible for initiating the slow-wave potential of the gastrointestinal tract located?
explanation:
The rhythmic contractions of the gastrointestinal (GI) tract are governed by underlying slow electrical waves. The primary pacemaker cells that generate these waves are the Interstitial Cells of Cajal (ICCs).

While ICCs are found throughout the GI tract, the dominant pacemaker that sets the fundamental rhythm is located in the midbody of the stomach along the greater curvature. These cells have the highest intrinsic frequency (approximately 3 waves per minute), and this rhythm, known as the Basic Electrical Rhythm (BER), propagates down the rest of the GI tract.

Explanation of Other Options:

Option B C and D: Although the duodenum, jejunum, and large intestine all have their own networks of Interstitial Cells of Cajal, they function as subsidiary pacemakers. They are entrained by and follow the primary rhythm set by the dominant pacemaker in the stomach. The intrinsic frequency of these subsidiary pacemakers is progressively lower down the GI tract (e.g., ~12/min in the duodenum, ~9/min in the jejunum).

Key Takeaways:

  • The pacemaker cells of the GI tract are the Interstitial Cells of Cajal (ICCs).
  • They generate the slow-wave potential or Basic Electrical Rhythm (BER).
  • The primary pacemaker with the highest frequency is located in the stomach.
  • The frequency of the BER decreases progressively from the stomach to the colon.

question_text: GFR will be increased if:

option_b: Decreased oncotic pressure in glomerular capillaries

Determinants of the GFR

  • Pressures in the capillaries are the major forces that govern fluid movement in them. Such forces are commonly called Starling forces
  • GFR is determined by,
    • Hydrostatic and colloid osmotic forces across the glomerular membrane that determines "Net filtration pressure"
    • Filtration coefficient, Kf

GFR = Kf *Net filtration pressure

  • Important pressures under consideration are,
    • Glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure, PG = 60 mm Hg
    • Hydrostatic pressure in Bowman's capsule (PB) = 18 mm Hg
    • Colloid osmotic pressure of the glomerular capillary plasma proteins (πG) = 32 mm Hg
    • The colloid osmotic pressure of the proteins in Bowman's capsule (πB) - In normal individuals, since albumin is not filtered, πB is zero

Forces Favoring Filtration (mm Hg)

  • Glomerular hydrostatic pressure = 60
  • Bowman's capsule colloid osmotic pressure = 0

Forces Opposing Filtration (mm Hg)

  • Bowman's capsule hydrostatic pressure = 18
  • Glomerular capillary colloid osmotic pressure = 32

Net filtration pressure = 60-18-32 = 10 mm Hg

  • Since Glomerular capillary colloid osmotic pressure oppose filtration, its decrease actually increases GFR

question_text: What is the typical Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) in a healthy adult?
explanation:
Explanation:

The standard average GFR for a healthy individual is 125 ml/min.

  • Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) is the rate at which plasma is filtered by the glomeruli in the kidneys.
  • It is akey indicator of kidney function.
  • The normal GFR range is around 90-120 ml/min/1.73 m2 for most adults, but 125 ml/min is considered the standard average for a healthy individual.
  • Theformula to calculate GFR is:

GFR = Net Filtration Pressure (NFP)×Filtration Coefficient (Kf)

Factors affecting GFR include:

  • Renal Blood Flow
    • Increased blood flow boosts GFR, while decreased blood flow reduces it.
  • Hydrostatic and Osmotic Pressures
    • High glomerular capillary pressure increases GFR, whereas high pressure in Bowman's capsule or elevated colloid osmotic pressure decreases it.
  • Constriction of Afferent and Efferent Arterioles
    • Constriction of afferent arterioles reduces GFR, while constriction of efferent arterioles can increase GFR.
  • Hormonal and Neural Controls
    • Various hormones like angiotensin II, and conditions, like sympathetic nervous system activation can modulate GFR by affecting blood flow and pressure within the kidneys.

question_text:
Which of the following statements is true about GFR?
GFR-Glomerular filtration rate
RPF-Renal Plasma Flow
option_a: An increase in sympathetic function increases GFR
option_c: An increase in RPF increases GFR
option_d: A decrease in RPF increases GFR
explanation:
Explanation:

An increase in renal plasma flow (RPF) enhances glomerular hydrostatic pressure, thereby promoting filtration and increasing GFR.

Mediators influencing GFR:

  • Prostaglandins (PGE2, PGI2): Increase GFR by vasodilation; counterbalance sympathetic and angiotensin II-induced vasoconstriction.
  • Bradykinin: Increases GFR through vasodilation.
  • Nitric Oxide: Promotes GFR and helps maintain sodium and water excretion; reduced NO is associated with hypertension.
  • Angiotensin II: Has a biphasic effect-mild efferent constriction increases GFR, but severe constriction eventually decreases it.
  • Sympathetic nerves, norepinephrine, epinephrine, endothelin: Cause vasoconstriction, generally reducing GFR.

Arteriolar changes and GFR:

  • Afferent arteriole constriction: Increases resistance → decreases glomerular pressure → lowers GFR.
  • Afferent arteriole dilation: Decreases resistance → increases glomerular pressure → raises GFR.
  • Efferent arteriole constriction (mild): Increases pressure → slight rise in GFR.
  • Efferent arteriole constriction (severe): Initially raises, but then reduces GFR due to increased colloid osmotic pressure.
  • Efferent arteriole dilation: Reduces glomerular pressure → decreases GFR.

Explanation of other options:

An increase in sympathetic function (Option A): Sympathetic activation causes vasoconstriction, especially of the afferent arteriole, reducing renal blood flow and GFR.

Afferent arteriolar constriction (Option B): Raises vascular resistance and lowers glomerular hydrostatic pressure, which decreases GFR rather than increasing it.

A decrease in RPF (Option D): Reducing renal plasma flow decreases the filtration pressure, which lowers GFR.

question_text: What renal function is represented by the formula UV/P?
explanation:
Explanation:

The formula UV/P, where U is the concentration of a substance in the urine, V is the urine flow rate, and P is the concentration of the substance in the plasma, represents the renal clearance of that substance.

Clearance

  • Clearance measures the volume of plasma completely cleared of a substance by the kidneys per minute (mL/min), reflecting renal excretory efficiency.
  • It is essential for evaluating kidney function, including filtration, reabsorption, and secretion processes.
  • To calculate the clearance rate (Cs) of the substance, use the formula:

where Cs is the clearance rate of a substance s, Ps is the plasma concentration of the substance, Us is the urine concentration of that substance, and V is the urine flow rate.

Inulin clearance

  • Inulin clearance can be used to estimate glomerular filtration rate.
  • If a substance is freely filtered and is not reabsorbed or secreted by the renal tubules, then the rate at which that substance is excreted in the urine (Us × V) is equal to the filtration rate of the substance by the kidneys (GFR × Ps).
  • A substance that fits these criteria is inulin, a polysaccharide molecule with a molecular weight of about 5200.
  • Inulin, which is not produced in the body, is found in the roots of certain plants and must be administered intravenously to a patient to measure GFR.

Creatinine clearance

  • Creatinine clearance can also be used to assess GFR.
  • Because measurement of creatinine clearance does not require intravenous infusion into the patient, this method is much more widely used than inulin clearance for estimating GFR clinically.

Para-­ aminohippuric acid clearance

  • Para-aminohippuric acid (PAH) is the best marker for estimating effective renal plasma flow.
  • Approximately 20% is filtered, and the remaining 80% is secreted, resulting in nearly complete excretion.
  • The clearance of PAH is approximately equal to the effective renal plasma flow.
  • Renal blood flow (RBF) can be calculated from renal plasma flow using the haematocrit: RBF = RPF / (1 -Haematocrit).

Explanation of other options:

Filtration (Option A): This process refers to the initial filtration of blood through the glomerulus to form filtrate. The formula does not measure this process directly.

Tubular Secretion (Option B): Tubular secretion is the process by which substances are actively transported from the blood into the renal tubules. The formula does not specifically measure tubular secretion.

Tubular Reabsorption (Option C): This refers to the process of reabsorbing substances from the renal tubules back into the blood. The formula does not measure reabsorption directly.

question_text:
A 22-year-old male college student volunteers for a research study involving renal function.
He undergoes several laboratory tests, the results of which are below:

What is the estimated renal blood flow?
explanation:
Renal blood flow (RBF) is the volume of blood that flows through the kidney per unit time. RBF is determined by the pressure difference between the renal artery and vein, and the resistance in the renal vasculature. Despite changes in the systemic blood pressure, the kidneys maintain a fairly steady RBF by modifying renal vascular resistance.

Because invasive direct measurement is not practical, RBF is calculated from the renal plasma flow (RPF) and hematocrit using the following equation:

RBF = RPF/(1 - hematocrit)

Because para-aminohippurate (PAH) is almost entirely removed from the blood as it passes through the kidney by both glomerular filtration and tubular secretion, PAH is a reflection of renal plasma flow.

PAH clearance, and therefore RBF, is calculated using the following equation: RBF = RPF/(1 - hematocrit)

Since para-aminohippurate (PAH) is almost entirely removed from the blood as it passes through the kidney, by both glomerular filtration and tubular secretion, it is a reflection of renal plasma flow.

PAH clearance, and therefore renal plasma flow, is then calculated using the following equation:

RPF = PAH clearance = [urine PAH]/[plasma PAH] x urine flow rate.

Combining the two equations:

RBF = (urine PAH]/[plasma PAH] x urine flow rate)/(1 - hematocrit) = (150 / 0.2 x 1)/(1- 0.5) = 1,500 mL/min.

Option A: 200 mL/min would be the result if inulin clearance was used instead of PAH. inulin clearance is used to estimate glomerular filtration rate (GFR) because inulin is freely filtered in the glomerulus, but neither reabsorbed nor secreted in the renal tubule.

Option B: 1000 mL/min can only result from an error in calculation.

Option D: 750 mL/min is the clearance of PAH or the renal plasma flow (RPF) rate. Because plasma is equal to biood minus the erythrocytes (red blood cells), the RPF can be used to calculate the RBF if hematocrit is known.

Learning objective: RBF can be calculated by using the hematocrit and PAH clearance as an estimate of RPF. RBF = RPF/(1 - hematocrit).

question_text: Which cells secrete renin?
explanation:
Explanation:

Renin is produced by juxtaglomerular (JG) cells, which are specialized smooth muscle cells found in the walls of the afferent arterioles of the kidney, near the glomerulus. These cells release renin in response to various signals such as decreased blood pressure, low sodium levels, or activation of the sympathetic nervous system.

Location of JG Cells: The juxtaglomerular cells are located in the afferent arteriole just before it enters the glomerulus. They form part of the juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA), a structure that helps regulate blood pressure and the filtration rate in the kidneys.

Triggers for Renin Release: Renin secretion by JG cells is stimulated by several factors:

  • A drop in blood pressure, detected by baroreceptors within the JG cells themselves.
  • Reduced sodium levels in the distal tubule, which are sensed by the macula densa.
  • Stimulation by the sympathetic nervous system via β-adrenergic receptors.

Role of Renin: Renin acts as an enzyme that kick-starts the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS). It converts angiotensinogen, a protein produced by the liver, into angiotensin I. Angiotensin I is then converted into angiotensin II in the lungs. Angiotensin II helps increase blood pressure by constricting blood vessels and triggering the secretion of aldosterone, a hormone that promotes sodium and water retention in the kidneys.

Explanation for other options:

Lacis cells (Option A): These are extraglomerular mesangial cells situated near the juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA). Although they support the function of the JG cells and are part of the JGA, they do not produce or secrete renin.

Macula densa (Option B): Located in the distal convoluted tubule, the macula densa cells monitor the sodium concentration in the filtrate. While they play a crucial role in signaling the JG cells to release renin when sodium levels drop, they themselves do not secrete renin.

Intraglomerular mesangial cells (Option D): Found within the glomerulus, these cells mainly provide structural support and help regulate blood flow, but they are not involved in renin secretion.

question_text:
A large pharmaceutical company is seeking healthy volunteers to participate in a drug trial. The drug is excreted in the urine and the volunteers must agree to laboratory testing before enrolling in the trial. The lab results of one volunteer are shown below:

Urinalysis test results:

Assuming an urine flow rate of 1 mUmin, which set of values below is the clearance of glucose, sodium, and creatinine in this patient?
option_a: Glucose: 0 mg/dL, sodium: 45 mUmin, creatinine: 100 mg/dL
option_b: Glucose: 0 mg/dL, sodium: 0.25 mUmin. creatinine: 100 mg/dL
option_c: Glucose: 0 mg/dL, sodium: 48 mUmin, creatinine: 100 mg/dL
option_d: Glucose: 148 mg/dL, sodium: 105 mUmin, creatinine: 99 mg/dL
explanation:
Clearance is a theoretical volume of plasma from which a substance is completely removed.

Clearance can be determined for any substance and is calculated using the following equation:

CI = K urine x V urine/K plasma (CI is clearance, K is concentration, and V is urine flow rate) Clearance calculations for glucose, sodium, and creatinine are as follows:

Cl glucose = 0 x 1/148 = 0 Cl sodium = 35 x 1/140 = 0.25 CI creatinine = 100 x 1/ 1=100 Several renal tubular mechanisms modulate the clearance of any substance:

Filtration

Some substances (inulin, PAH, and creatinine) are freely filtered and not reabsorbed from the tubule, thus will have a high renal clearance. In contrast, plasma proteins are not filtered and have zero clearance in normal, healthy kidneys.

Secretion

Some substances (PAH and creatinine) are actively secreted into the tubule will have a high renal clearance if not reabsorbed.

* Reabsorption - Most of the normal physiologic constituents of plasma (electrolytes and water) are reabsorbed to various degrees in the proximal convoluted tubule of the nephron. Several substances (glucose and amino acids) are freely filtered, but entirely reabsorbed from the tubule and therefore have zero clearance under normal circumstances.

question_text: A 40-year-old man with suspected hemolytic anemia undergoes urine analysis, which shows no free hemoglobin under normal physiological conditions. This is because hemoglobin is normally unable to cross the glomerular filtration barrier. Which of the following best explains this finding?
option_a: It is a large molecule bound with another protein
option_b: It gets attracted to the negative charge of the glomerular filtration barrier
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Hemoglobin is a tetrameric protein with a molecular weight of ~64,500 Da.
  • In the circulation, free hemoglobin released from red blood cells rapidly binds to haptoglobin, forming an even larger complex.
  • The glomerular filtration barrier normally prevents filtration of proteins above ~70 kDa.
  • Hence, hemoglobin-haptoglobin complexes are too large to be filtered, explaining why hemoglobin is not normally present in urine.

Explanation of Other Options:

Negative charge barrier (Option B): The glomerular basement membrane is negatively charged and restricts filtration of negatively charged proteins like albumin. Hemoglobin, however, is not primarily blocked by charge-it is excluded due to size.

Both A and B (Option C): Incorrect because the main limiting factor for hemoglobin is molecular size/complex formation, not charge.

None of the above (Option D): Incorrect since option A is correct.

Key Take Away Points:

  1. Structure of Glomerular Filtration Barrier
    • Endothelium: Fenestrated, allows plasma water & small solutes.
    • Basement membrane: Dense mesh of collagen + glycoproteins (negatively charged).
    • Podocytes with slit diaphragms: Size-selective barrier.
  2. Determinants of Filtration
  3. Clinical Correlation:
    • Hemoglobinuria occurs only when plasma haptoglobin is saturated (e.g., intravascular hemolysis in malaria, mismatched transfusion, severe burns).
    • Albuminuria in minimal change disease results from loss of the negative charge barrier, not size.

question_text: The macula densa is a specialised group of epithelial cells in the distal tubules of the nephron. It a part of the juxtaglomerular apparatus. A decrease in NaCl at the macula densa would cause which of the following?
option_a: Increased renin secretion and increased afferent arteriolar resistance
option_b: Decreased renin secretion and decreased afferent arteriolar resistance
option_c: Increased renin secretion and decrease afferent arteriolar resistance
option_d: Decrease renin secretion and increased afferent arteriolar resistance
explanation:
Option C: In response to low GFR, the macula densa acts as an auto regulator and increases the GFR. Decreased GFR decreases the flow in the tubule, which allows for more sodium reabsorption. This decreases the NaCl at macula densa. This causes the release of renin, which increases angiotensin II which in turn increases the efferent arteriolar resistance, ultimately increasing the GFR.

A decrease in afferent arteriolar resistance allows more blood in the glomerular capillaries and thus increases the hydrostatic pressure in them. An increased hydrostatic pressure increases the filtration and thus the GFR.

Option A: Increased renin secretion and increased afferent arteriolar resistance: Incorrect, as decreased NaCl actually leads to decreased afferent arteriolar resistance.

Option B: Decreased renin secretion and decreased afferent arteriolar resistance: Incorrect, since a decrease in NaCl triggers an increase in renin secretion.

Option D: Decreased renin secretion and increased afferent arteriolar resistance: Incorrect, as decreased NaCl causes increased renin secretion rather than decreased.

Key takeaways:

Decreased NaCl at the macula densa increases renin secretion and decreases afferent arteriolar resistance, enhancing glomerular filtration.

question_text: What causes a decrease in glomerular filtration rate (GFR)?
explanation:
Explanation:

GFR depends on the filtration surface area and membrane permeability, both represented by the glomerular filtration coefficient (Kf).

A decrease in Kf occurs due to glomerular damage, basement membrane thickening, or mesangial contraction, leading to reduced filtration.

Conditions like CKD and diabetic nephropathy reduce Kf, causing decreased GFR.

Factors Affecting GFR

Explanation of other options:

Decrease in glomerular oncotic pressure (Option B): Incorrect because this would increase filtration and GFR.

Increase in glomerular hydrostatic pressure (Option C): Incorrect because higher PGC enhances filtration, raising GFR.

Decrease of Bowman's hydrostatic pressure (Option D): Incorrect because lower PBS facilitates filtration, increasing GFR.

Key Takeaways:

  • ↓ Kf = ↓ GFR (seen in chronic renal disease).
  • ↑ PGC → ↑ GFR; ↑ πG or ↑ PBS → ↓ GFR.
  • Kf reflects surface area and permeability.

This increased reabsorption of sodium decreases sodium delivery to the macula densa, which elicits a tubuloglomerular feedback-mediated increase in GFR, allowing Na excretion to remain normal with increased excretion of waste products of protein metabolism.

Key takeaways:

A protein-rich diet increases GFR due to enhanced renal blood flow while sodium excretion typically remains normal.

question_text:
A 36-year-old man presents with the complaint of loose and watery stools for the past 3 days. He is now having bowel movements four to five times a day. He denies any blood or mucus in the stool. He also complains of abdominal pain and fatigue.
Furthermore, he feels nauseous and does not feel like drinking anything. His urine is visibly yellow and low in volume. He recently returned from a trip to South America where he enjoyed all the local delicacies.
He is most concerned about his urine color and volume. Which segment of the nephron is primarily responsible for these changes?
explanation:
This patient's urine is yellow and low in volume as it is concentrated and hyperosmotic. Concentrated urine is produced due to countercurrent multiplication in the loop of Henle, as explained here:

Descending limb: Permeable to water; impermeable to solutes; water leaves the tubule through aquaporins (specialized channels for water transport found in nearly all cells of the body)

Thin ascending limb: impermeable to water (lacks aquaporins) and solutes; NaCl is actively pumped into interstitium to create hypertonic environment

Thick ascending limb: Na+/K+/2Cl cotransporter actively transports solutes into the interstium; alone this pump can only create about a 200 mOsm/L concentration gradient

The countercurrent flow between the descending and ascending limbs is primarily responsible for the 1200 mOsm/L gradient at the bottom of the loop of Henle in the innermost part of the renal medulla Vasa recta, blood vessels of the renal medulla, are responsible for removing solutes and water and help maintain the concentration gradient

The following diagram helps explain the establishment of the gradient:

Option A: The glomerulus is responsible for fittering water and solutes from the plasma into the renal tubule. It does not play any further role in concentrating or diluting the final urine that is produced.

Option B: The proximal convoluted tubule (pars convoluta) is responsible for the active reabsorption of the nutrients, like amino acids and glucose, that are filtered into the tubule. Obligatory sodium reabsorption along with passive water and chloride reabsorption also occurs in this segment.

Option C: The proximal straight tubule (pars recta) is the terminal portion of the proximal tubule and is responsible primarily for reabsorbing electrolytes from the tubuiar fluid.

Learning objective: Countercurrent multiplication in the loop of Henle is primarily responsible for the urine concentrating ability of the nephron.

question_text: Which of the following sites is responsible for the greatest amount of water reabsorption?
explanation:
Explanation:

Most water reabsorption takes place in the proximal tubule. Around 65-70% of the filtered water is reabsorbed here, along with sodium, glucose, and other substances. This process mainly occurs through osmosis, driven by the active reabsorption of solutes like sodium.

  • Filtration: Blood is filtered in the glomerulus, producing filtrate that enters the proximal tubule, containing water, sodium, glucose, urea, and other small molecules.
  • Reabsorption in the proximal tubule: Approximately 65-70% of filtered water is reabsorbed passively by osmosis, following the active reabsorption of solutes such as sodium, glucose, and bicarbonate.
  • Sodium, glucose, and bicarbonate: These solutes are actively reabsorbed along with water, which helps maintain fluid and electrolyte balance.
  • Mechanism: Proximal tubule cells use sodium-potassium ATPase pumps to create a sodium gradient, enabling active transport of sodium (and other solutes) into the interstitial space. Water then follows passively by osmosis to maintain osmotic equilibrium.

Explanation for other options:

Loop of Henle (Option B): The loop of Henle is important for urine concentration. The descending limb is permeable to water and allows some water reabsorption, while the ascending limb is impermeable to water. However, only about 20-25% of water reabsorption takes place here.

Distal convoluted tubule (Option C): The distal convoluted tubule fine-tunes the reabsorption of sodium and water but is not the main site of water reabsorption. A small amount of water is reabsorbed here, regulated by hormones such as aldosterone and antidiuretic hormone (ADH).

Collecting duct (Option D): The collecting duct also plays a role in water reabsorption, especially under the influence of ADH, and is crucial for determining the final urine concentration based on the body's hydration status. However, it is not the site where most of the water reabsorption occurs.

question_text: A 25-year-old man returning from a country with endemic malaria was given primaquine for prevention of malaria. Shortly after starting the drug, he presented with dark urine. Which of the following effects did primaquine have on his red blood cells?
option_a: It damaged the cells by acting as a free radical scavenger or antioxidant.
option_b: It exerted more oxidative stress on his red blood cells than the cells could handle.
option_c: It inhibited G6PD and therefore led to an increase in the concentration of oxidized glutathione.
option_d: It irreversibly reduced oxidized glutathione to GSH.
explanation:
G6PD Deficiency: Leads to reduced NADPH production, which is crucial for maintaining reduced glutathione (GSH).

Option B: Oxidative Stress: In individuals with G6PD deficiency, primaquine increases oxidative stress beyond what their red blood cells can manage.

Result: This leads to hemolysis, which explains the presentation of dark urine due to hemoglobinuria.

Why not other options:

Option A: It Damaged the Cells by Acting as a Free Radical Scavenger or Antioxidant: This is incorrect as primaquine does not act as an antioxidant; instead, it increases oxidative stress in G6PD-deficient individuals.

Option C: It Inhibited G6PD and Therefore Led to an Increase in the Concentration of Oxidized Glutathione: Primaquine does not inhibit G6PD; rather, it causes oxidative stress due to the lack of reduced glutathione, resulting from G6PD deficiency.

Option D: It Irreversibly Reduced Oxidized Glutathione to GSH: This is misleading as primaquine does not directly reduce oxidized glutathione to GSH; instead, it exacerbates oxidative stress, leading to hemolysis in G6PD-deficient individuals.

Key takeaways:

After starting primaquine, the 25-year-old man experienced dark urine due to oxidative stress on his red blood cells, which exceeded their capacity to manage it, especially in the context of G6PD deficiency.

question_text: Where does the majority of water absorption occur within the renal tubules?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The majority of water reabsorption within the renal tubules occurs in the Proximal Convoluted Tubule (PCT).
  • Approximately 65-70% of the filtered water is reabsorbed in the PCT.
  • This reabsorption process is critical for maintaining fluid balance and involves the active transport of sodium ions, which creates an osmotic gradient that drives water reabsorption.
  • The PCT also reabsorbs other essential substances such as glucose, amino acids, and electrolytes, contributing to the overall homeostasis of the body.
  • The high capacity of the proximal tubule for reabsorption results from
    • Increased number of mitochondria
    • Extensive brush border on the luminal side of membrane
  • In PCT water reabsorption occurs via osmosis through aquaporin-1 channels. Aquaporin-1 is the main water channel present in the PCT & Loop of Henle.
  • Water reabsorption in the PCT is obligatory (around two-thirds), while water reabsorption in the collecting duct under the influence of ADH is facultative.

Explanation of other options:

Distal Convoluted Tubule (Option B): DCT is responsible for fine-tuning the reabsorption of sodium and water, but it does not account for the majority of water reabsorption. It primarily adjusts the concentration of urine in response to hormonal signals.

Loop of Henle (LOH) (Option C): The Loop of Henle plays a significant role in establishing the medullary osmotic gradient, crucial for water reabsorption in the collecting duct, but does not absorb the majority of water.

Collecting Duct (Option D): While the collecting duct is responsible for the final adjustments in water reabsorption under the influence of antidiuretic hormone (ADH), the majority of water absorption largely occurs in PCT.

question_text: A 25-year-old man undergoes renal function testing after a history of severe dehydration. Analysis of his proximal tubular fluid shows that the concentrations of glucose, amino acids, and bicarbonate decrease significantly compared to plasma. However, the concentration of one ion appears relatively higher in the tubular fluid as it passes through the proximal convoluted tubule. Which ion is it?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • In the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT), nearly 65-70% of filtered solutes and water are reabsorbed.
  • Glucose and amino acids are almost completely reabsorbed via Na+-dependent secondary active transport.
  • Bicarbonate is reabsorbed after conversion to CO2 by carbonic anhydrase; ~85% of filtered HCO3is reabsorbed in PCT.
  • Chloride, however, is reabsorbed more slowly compared to sodium and water in the early PCT. As water leaves the lumen, C- becomes relatively concentrated in the tubular fluid (TF/P ratio increases).
  • Thus, unlike glucose, amino acids, and bicarbonate, chloride concentration does not decrease significantly in early PCT.

Explanation of Other Options:

Amino acid (Option A): Completely reabsorbed in early PCT by Na+-amino acid symporters → concentration falls sharply.

Glucose (Option B): Fully reabsorbed via SGLT-2 & SGLT-1 transporters in early PCT → concentration falls to near zero.

Bicarbonate (Option D): 80-90% reabsorbed in PCT via carbonic anhydrase-mediated mechanism → concentration decreases.

Key Take Away Points:

  1. Reabsorptive Profile of PCT
  1. Concept of TF/P Ratio (Tubular Fluid/Plasma Ratio)
  • TF/P < 1: Solute reabsorbed faster than water (e.g., glucose, amino acids, HCO3-).
  • TF/P > 1: Solute reabsorbed more slowly than water (e.g., Cl-, urea).
  • TF/P ≈ 1: Solute reabsorbed proportionally to water (e.g., Na+, K+).
  1. Clinical Correlation:
  • In diabetes mellitus, glucose reabsorption saturates (exceeds Tm) → glucosuria.
  • Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (acetazolamide) block HCO3- reabsorption in PCT → metabolic acidosis + alkaline urine.

question_text: Which of the following statements about renal tubular transport is correct?

Urea is absorbed 100% in the PCT (Option B): Urea is only partially reabsorbed in the PCT. Most urea reabsorption happens later in the loop of Henle and distal tubule, where it plays a critical role in urine concentration.

H+ is absorbed in the proximal tubule (Option C): Hydrogen ions (H+) are not absorbed in the PCT; instead, they are secreted into the tubular lumen to help regulate acid-base balance.

question_text:
A healthy volunteer who is enrolled in a clinical study receives multiple daily doses of substance X that is not metabolized in the body, but is freely filtered and undergoes secretion in the renal tubules with minimal reabsorption.
Renal studies show the following:

What is the plasma concentration of substance X in the volunteer?
explanation:
• Filtered load = GFR x plasma conc of drug X
    • absolute amount of load that is delivered to Bowman's space in glomerulus
    • reflects the amount of substance that is initially filtered into tubule
  • Excretion = filtered load + net tubular transport
    • Filtered load = excretion - net tubular transport
  • combining both equations
    • excretion - net tubular transport = GFR x plasma conc of drug X (P)
    • [GFR= inulin clearance]

question_text: Positive lumen gradient for absorption of divalent-ions in thick ascending loop of henle, is by recycling of which of the following ion?
explanation:
Positive lumen gradient for absorption of divalent ions in a thick ascending loop of henle is by recycling of potassium (K+) ions.

An Important component of solute reabsorption in the thick ascending limb is the Na+-K+ ATPase pump in the epithelial cell basolateral membranes.

In the thick ascending loop, movement of sodium across the luminal membrane is mediated primarily by a 1-sodium, 2-chloride, 1-potassium cotransporter (NKCC2). The thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle is the site of action of the loop diuretics furosemide, ethacrynic acid, and bumetanide, all of which inhibit the action of the NKCC2 cotransporter.

There is also significant paracellular reabsorption of cations, such as Mg2+, Ca2+, Na+, and K+, in the thick ascending limb as a result of the slight positive charge of the tubular lumen relative to the interstitial fluid.

Although the NKCC2 cotransporter moves equal amounts of catIons and anions into the cell, there is a slight backleak of potassium ions into the lumen, creating a positive charge of about +8 millivolts in the tubular lumen.

question_text: In a 40-year-old man, there is chronic Na+ loss in the urine, with resultant hypovolemia, hypokalaemia and alkalosis due to defective transport in the thick ascending limb. What is the probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Option B: Thick ascending limb of loop of Henle has Na+ 2Cl - K+ co transporter that cotransports one Na+, one K+, and 2Cl- from the tubular lumen into the tubular cells. Na K ATPase in the basolateral membrane of the cell, transports Na+ out of the cell into the interstitium. Cl- exits in basolateral CIC-Kb channels. Barttin, a protein in the cell membrane, is essential for normal CIC-Kb function. K+ moves from the cell to the interstitium and the tubular lumen by ROMK (renal outer medullary potassium channel) and other K+ channels.

Bartter syndrome is due to defective transport in the thick ascending limb. It is characterized by chronic Na+ loss in the urine, with resultant hypovolemia causing stimulation of renin and aldosterone secretion without hypertension, plus hyperkalemia and alkalosis. The condition can be caused by loss-of-function mutations in the gene for any of four key proteins: The Na-K-2Cl cotransporter, the ROMK K+ channel, the ClC-Kb Cl- channel, or barttin, a recently described integral membrane protein that is necessary for the normal function of ClC-Kb Cl- channels.

Option A: Liddle syndrome: Caused by mutations leading to increased sodium reabsorption(ENaC) in the distal nephron, resulting in hypertension and hypokalemia, not hypovolemia.

Option C: Gitelman syndrome: Characterized by hypomagnesemia, hypocalcemia, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis due to a defect in the thiazide-sensitive Na-Cl cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule, not the thick ascending limb.

Option D: Dent syndrome: A rare X-linked disorder associated with low molecular weight proteinuria, hypercalciuria, and renal stones, not primarily characterized by chronic Na+ loss or hypovolemia.

Key takeaways:

Bartter syndrome is due to defective sodium transport in the thick ascending limb, causing chronic Na+ loss, hypovolemia, hypokalemia, and alkalosis.

question_text: Role of Vasa recta
explanation:
Countercurrent multiplier - "Loop of Henle"

  • Thin descending loop of Henle "the concentrating segment"
    • We know that that the fluid leaves out of PCT is isosomotic (300 mosm/kg)
    • Once it enters the descending loop of Henle (dLOH), water moves out freely leaving the solutes inside. The fluid in the descending limb of the loop of Henle becomes hypertonic
    • The osmolarity reached at the tip of dLOH is around 1200 mosm/kg
    • Water moves out of the dLOH through aquaporin1
  • Thick ascending loop of Henle - "the diluting segment"
    • Thick ascending loop of Henle is permeable to solutes and impermeable to water
    • Sodium, chloride and potassium moves out of the thick ascending limb through Na-K-2Cl cotransporter
    • Because of selective movement of solutes leaving water inside fluid inside thick ascending limb becomes hypotonic to plasma

Countercurrent exchanger - "Vasa recta"

  • Vasa recta are straight capillaries that run parallel to loop of Henle
  • Vasa recta serves as countercurrent exchanger- they minimize washout of solutes and maintain the osmolarity gradient developed by loop of Henle

question_text: All the following are mechanisms of action of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) EXCEPT?
option_a: Increase absorption of urea in the medullary collecting duct
option_b: Increase absorption of urea in the descending loop of Henle
option_c: Decrease absorption of NaCl in the ascending loop of Henle
option_d: Increase water permeability in the collecting ducts
explanation:
Explanation:

ADH does not act on the descending loop of Henle.

  • ADH (vasopressin) acts mainly on the collecting ductsby inserting aquaporin-2 channels, thereby increasing water reabsorption and producing concentrated urine. (Option D ruled out)
  • It also increases urea permeabilityin the inner medullary collecting ducts, which helps maintain medullary hyperosmolarity and enhances water reabsorption. (Option A ruled out)
  • ADH also reduces NaCl reabsorption in the thick ascending loop of Henle, indirectly supporting urine concentration.(Option C ruled out)

Key Takeaways:

  • Site of ADH action:Distal tubules & collecting ducts.
  • Main effects:↑ water permeability, ↑ urea reabsorption (inner medullary CD), ↓ NaCl reabsorption (thick ascending limb).
  • No action on the descending limb of Henle(permeable to water but independent of ADH).

question_text: Macula densa formed by which part of nephron
explanation:
• Macula densa is made up of specialised cells located at the junction of thick ascending limb and Distal convoluted tubule (DCT).
  • They are modified epithelial cells present at the distal end of thick ascending limb of Loop of Henle (LOH) when it comes in contact with the afferent and efferent arterioles.

  • It provides an appropriate feedback signal to the renal corpuscle to change the rate of filtration so that it can meet the need of the kidney functions.

question_text: Which among the following is not used in the Sahli method of hemoglobin estimation?
explanation:
Explanation:

In Sahli's (acid hematin) method, hemoglobin is estimated by converting it into acid hematin using N/10 hydrochloric acid. The Sahli's hemoglobinometer consists of the following main components:

  • Comparator with brown standard glasses for color matching
  • Sahli's pipette (20 μL) used to draw and add the blood sample
  • Graduated hemoglobin (Sahli-Adams) tube, marked in g% and percentage, where dilution and color matching are performed
  • Stirrer for mixing the contents

Therefore, the RBC pipette (used in RBC counting with hemocytometer) is not a part of the Sahli method apparatus.


Explanation of other options:

Comparator with brown standard (Option B): Used for color comparison of the acid hematin solution to determine hemoglobin concentration.

Sahli pipette (Option C): A 20 μL pipette used to deliver an accurate volume of blood into the hemoglobin tube.

Graduated Hb tube (Option D): Contains the diluting acid (N/10 HCl) and the converted acid hematin solution for visual comparison and reading.

Key Takeaways:

  • Sahli's method = Acid hematin method (visual comparator-based).
  • Components: Comparator, Sahli pipette, Hb tube, Stirrer.
  • RBC pipette is not used in this method.
  • Modern methods (e.g., Cyanmethemoglobin method) provide more accuracy and reliability.

References: https://laboratorytests.org/sahlis-method/

question_text: A 56-year-old man is suffering from hypertension for which he is given hydrochlorthiazide belonging to thiazide group of diuretic. This drug will act on which segment of the renal tubule?
explanation:
Option D: The thiazide diuretics, which are widely used to treat disorders such as hypertension and heart failure, inhibit the sodium-chloride co-transporter. It acts on this cotransporter in the distal tubules.

Option A: Proximal convoluted tubule: Thiazide diuretics do not act here; they primarily affect the distal convoluted tubule. Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors act here.

Option B: Collecting duct: This segment is targeted by potassium-sparing diuretics, not thiazides.

Option C: Ascending loop of Henle: Loop diuretics (e.g., furosemide) act here, whereas thiazides do not.

Key takeaways:

Thiazide diuretics, like hydrochlorothiazide, act on the distal convoluted tubule, inhibiting the sodium-chloride co-transporter.

question_text:
A 66-year-old man presents to the emergency department for shortness of breath for the last 2 hours. Despite his diagnosis of heart failure 2 years ago, he has refused to make any diet changes. He takes aspirin and carvedilol but is poorly compliant. His vitals signs are pulse of 135/min, respirations 30/min, and a blood pressure of 150/80 mm Hg.
The patient is visibly distressed and unable to lie down. He is taking shaliow breaths and auscultation reveals bilateral crackles in the chest. Jugular venous distension is seen. Pitting edema is present in the lower limbs.
A chest X-ray shows prominent interstitial markings bilaterally with alveolar infiltrates. Which of the following is the mechanism of action of the drug that can relieve his ongoing symptoms?
option_a: Acting on the B-adrenergic receptors to increase cardiac contractility.
option_b: By holding water within the tubule, leading to osmotic diuresis.
option_c: Blocking the Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle.
option_d: Blocking the angiotensin I receptors, leading to vasodilation. Blocking the NaCl channels in the distal tubule of the nephron.
explanation:
This patient has decompensated congestive heart failure (CHF) leading to acute pulmonary edema. Other causes of acute pulmonary edema include myocardial infarction, mitral stenosis, mitral regurgitation, aortic insufficiency, and renovascular hypertension. The typical signs are:

Tachypnea

Shallow breaths

Tachycardia

Hypertension

Visible anxiety/distress

Worsening shortness of breath on lying down

Jugular venous distension

Fine crackles (crepitations) on auscultation The treatment of acute pulmonary edema includes loop diuretics, such as furosemide and ethacrynic acid, which inhibit the Na*-K*-2Cl- cotransporter located in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle.

The increased solute load within the tubule causes water to be retained and eventually excreted along with the solutes. Furthermore, blockage of the cotransporter interrupts the countercurrent multiplication needed to maintain the hypertonic renal medulla responsible for concentrating the urine.

Water is retained within the tubule and this mechanism is responsible for the very potent diuretic effect seen with loop diuretics. Potential adverse effects of furosemide include hypokalemia, hypocalcemia, alkalosis, ototoxicity, volume depletion, and nephritis.

Option A: α-agonists do increase cardiac contractility but also increase myocardial oxygen demand. The increased workload on the heart will worsen the cardiac failure and, therefore, the pulmonary edema. Beta blockers, like carvedilol, are recommended for CHF rather than beta agonists.

Option B: Osmotic diuretics, such as mannitol, are filtered by the glomerulus and pass through the tubule while retaining water. Mannitol is sometimes used to reduce raised intraocular pressure in glaucoma and to promote diuresis in patients at risk for acute renal failure. Osmotic diuretics are not used for the treatment of acute pulmonary edema.

Option D: Angiotensin-receptor blockers (ARBs), such as losartan, telmisartan, and valsartan, act by blocking angiotensin II receptors. They act by causing direct vasodilation in the blood vessels and reducing production of aldosterone in the renal cortex. They are used as antihypertensive drugs, in particular as alternatives for patients who cannot tolerate Angiotensin Converting Enzyme (ACE) inhibitors due to the common side effect of dry cough. ARBs are not indicated for the management of acute pulmonary edema.

Learning objective: Furosemide and other loop diuretics act by inhibiting the Na-K-2CI cotransporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle. This cotransporter Is responsible for maintaining the hypertonicity of the renal interstitium required to concentrate urine.

question_text: A 50-year-old man presents to the clinic with complaints of unilateral breast enlargement and tenderness on the left side. His medical history includes chronic liver disease due to alcohol abuse. Laboratory tests reveal low testosterone levels, elevated estradiol levels, and normal levels of luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH). Which of the following is the most likely physiological mechanism leading to gynecomastia in this patient?
option_b: Increased production of androgens due to adrenal hyperplasia
option_c: Increased sensitivity of estrogen receptors in breast tissue
option_d: Elevated levels of free testosterone due to reduced sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG)
explanation:
• Decreased hepatic metabolism of oestrogens:
    • Mechanism: Chronic liver disease impairs the liver's ability to metabolize and clear oestrogens from circulation, resulting in elevated oestradiol levels.
    • Hormonal Imbalance: This hormonal imbalance, characterized by low testosterone and high oestradiol, favours the development of gynecomastia.

Why not the other options?

  • B) Increased production of androgens due to adrenal hyperplasia:
    • Explanation: While adrenal hyperplasia can elevate androgen levels, this patient's hormonal profile shows low testosterone and elevated estrogens, indicating that increased androgens are not the primary cause of gynecomastia.
  • C) Increased sensitivity of estrogen receptors in breast tissue:
    • Explanation: Although sensitivity of estrogen receptors can contribute to gynecomastia, the primary issue in this case is the hormonal imbalance resulting from liver dysfunction, rather than a change in receptor sensitivity.
  • D) Elevated levels of free testosterone due to reduced sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG):
    • Explanation: While SHBG may be reduced in liver disease, this patient has low total testosterone levels, indicating that elevated free testosterone is not a contributing factor to his gynecomastia.

Key Takeaways:

  • Gynecomastia in this patient is primarily due to decreased hepatic metabolism of estrogens, resulting in elevated estradiol levels in the context of low testosterone.
  • Chronic liver disease significantly impacts hormone levels, leading to an imbalance that favours gynecomastia development.
